intro: Machinists run precise equipment, check quality and solve problems on the shop floor, skills that maintenance and installation trades reward. The closest of the 25 careers below is CNC tool operation, with an 88% skill match, while Industrial Machinery Mechanics are 85% matched and earn a BLS May 2025 median of $64,520, or 10% more.
why_it_works: Making parts to tight tolerances means reading drawings, setting up machines and measuring every piece. O*NET rates operation and control at 3.25 out of 5 for machinists and operations monitoring at 3.12. Machinery repair, aircraft assembly and millwright work use the same precision. All 25 matches need no extra education. The skills to add are maintaining, repairing and installing equipment.
tips: Move into maintenance: millwrights earn $65,700, which is 12% more, and fix the machines you run.
Elevator and Escalator Installers and Repairers earn $109,910, or 87% more, through apprenticeships.
Avionics Technicians earn $82,280, which is 40% more, and value your attention to tolerances.

faq.q: What jobs can former machinists do?
faq.a: The closest matches are CNC tool operators (88%), Industrial Machinery Mechanics (85%) and aircraft structure and systems assemblers (83%), based on O*NET 31.0. Aircraft assemblers earn $65,380, which is 11% more than the $58,750 machinist median, and use the same blueprint skills.

faq.q: Which careers for machinists pay more?
faq.a: 17 of the 25 matches pay more. Elevator installers earn $109,910 (87% more), transportation equipment electricians $84,890 (44% more) and Avionics Technicians $82,280 (40% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Most of these train through apprenticeships or employer programs.

faq.q: Do machinists need more education to switch?
faq.a: No. All 25 matches need no more education than machinists already have, including all of the top 10. A post-secondary certificate is common in close matches, held by 47% of workers in one of them, so short programs are the usual route.

The skills that most often need work are equipment maintenance, repairing, installation and managing financial resources. Quality control already rates 3 out of 5 for machinists in O*NET, so learning to maintain and repair machines is the main step toward better-paid trades.
